Online Return

Trust tax return

A trust return is the last step of a process that starts before 30 June. The trustee has to decide who is entitled to the year’s income, record that decision in time, and report it correctly. Beneficiaries then pay tax on their share. We handle the resolution, the accounts and the return as one job.

Our fee

from $749 inc. GST

Fixed, covering the resolution, accounts and trust return.

Key date

30 June

For most discretionary trusts, the distribution resolution has to be made by year end.

Who does it

A registered tax agent

BRS Advisory Pty Ltd, Registered Tax Agent, CPA Australia Public Practice. Every client ID-verified before work starts.

What’s included

  • Estimate of the year’s income ahead of 30 June
  • Trustee distribution resolution drafted to your deed
  • Trust financial statements
  • Trust tax return prepared and lodged
  • Beneficiary statements and TFN reporting for closely held trusts
  • Distributions carried into beneficiaries’ own returns

How it runs

  1. 01 Verify identity online — each director, trustee or controlling owner does a three-minute check on their phone, included in the fee. Every client, every service, no exceptions. How it works.
  2. 02 In May or June, we estimate the income and talk through who should receive it.
  3. 03 The trustee signs the resolution before 30 June.
  4. 04 After year end we prepare the accounts and the return to match the resolution.
  5. 05 The trust and beneficiary returns are approved and lodged in step.

Why the resolution matters so much

If the trustee doesn’t make a valid resolution in time, the trust’s income can end up going to the default beneficiaries named in the deed. Or the trustee can be assessed on it at the top marginal rate. Neither is usually what anyone intended, and the resolution can’t be backdated. It’s the single most expensive thing to get wrong with a discretionary trust, and it’s entirely avoidable with a reminder in June.

Distributions that don’t reach the beneficiary

Distributing income to a beneficiary on a low tax rate, while the money is actually kept or used by someone else, can fall under section 100A. The ATO has been active in this area. Distributions to adult children, and to companies, get particular attention. We look at where the money actually goes as well as who is named in the resolution.

If you haven’t set a trust up yet

A trust adds a return, a resolution and an annual fee to your year. It can be worth it, for asset protection or flexibility in distributing business income, but not in every case. Our trust setup page covers whether a trust suits you and what establishing one involves.

Get a quote

Tell us about the trust, its income and its beneficiaries, and we’ll come back with a fixed fee. If it’s before 30 June, tell us that too.
